transcript:
<header>
Date: 2026-01-15
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood Solutions), Maya Chen (CloudScale CTO), Liam O'Neal (CloudScale Backend Lead), Sofia Petrov (CloudScale SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on throughput tuning: interleaved/continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token ceilings/floors), KV cache warmup/hitrate strategies, quantization tradeoffs on throughput and tail latency, and constraints for VPC/on-prem deployments.

Topics:
- Continuous batching heuristics and interleaved request handling
- Priority windows and token flood control (token ceil/floor)
- max_num_seqs and its interactions with per-tenant fairness
- KV cache warmup, prefetching, and eviction strategies
- Quantization (int8/int4) impact on kernel selection and batching
- VPC/on-prem constraints: NIC, NVLink, and node packing

Action items (captured briefly):
- Run KV warmup benchmark in their staging VPC
- Share scheduler knob matrix and prescriptive defaults
- Customer to provide traffic trace for replay

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone, thanks for blocking time. We, uh, want to focus on throughput tuning today — specifically how continuous batching and the scheduler knobs interplay when you have a mix of short chat-style calls and long document completion calls. Maya, thanks for joining, can you give quick context on your workload?
[00:18] Maya Chen: Sure, yep. Our main production workload is two-fold: short queries for search rerank and longer generation for summarization. Peak QPS is about 1.2k with spikes to 3k for 10-15 minutes most days. Latency SLO is 150ms p50 for short queries and 1.2s p95 for long ones. We're currently on MajorCloudAI managed GPUs, thinking about dedicated nodes or a VPC/private deployment to control data residency.
[00:42] Liam O'Neal: Just to add, we see a lot of token bursts — many short requests but some large ones with 2k tokens. Also we do few-shot prompts which blow up token counts occasionally. So token accounting and limits are a pain.
[00:58] Priya Rao: That mix is exactly where scheduler configs matter. Two knobs you should watch: continuous_batching_window and max_num_seqs. One controls how long the runtime tries to aggregate tokens, the other caps the number of concurrent sequences packed in a batch. If you set max_num_seqs too low you lose throughput; too high and you get head-of-line blocking or tail latency surprises.
[01:22] Sofia Petrov: Quick q — is max_num_seqs per-GPU or per-tenant slot? We have multi-tenant nodes in our staging cluster.
[01:28] Priya Rao: Good question. It's per-executor (so per-GPU slot) in Redwood's scheduler. For multi-tenant pools we recommend pairing it with tenant-priority windows and per-tenant token ceilings so no single tenant consumes the max_num_seqs budget for long completions.
[01:40] Diego Alvarez: Another nuance — the runtime supports interleaved batching where short requests are prioritized into early micro-batches while long sequences are appended to background buckets. That reduces p50 for short queries while still getting some packing benefits for long ones.
[01:55] Maya Chen: That sounds promising. How do you handle token flood — like when 400 concurrent short requests arrive, each 8 tokens? Won't they fill batches and starve longer sequences?
[02:06] Alex Mercer: Token flood control is done via token ceilings (a dynamic limit per-flow) and priority windows. We set a token_floor and token_ceil; the scheduler will cap how many tokens a single request can occupy in the aggregate batch. Also, we have admission controls: when burstiness exceeds a threshold, requests are shunted to a lower-priority queue or to a cheaper model variant.
[02:29] Liam O'Neal: Admission control — does that mean rejecting or delaying? In our app, dropping requests is not acceptable.
[02:34] Priya Rao: We usually delay or re-route to a faster, smaller model (e.g., 7b quantized) as a graceful degradation. In enterprise Dedicated mode you can also configure burst capacity with reserved extra slots for emergencies.
[02:47] Sofia Petrov: Regarding KV cache, our long completions rely heavily on a warm KV to avoid recomputation. How aggressive should prefetch be for our pattern?
[02:56] Priya Rao: For your mix, we recommend a two-step approach: short prefetch windows on cold starts (e.g., prewarm top-k tokens) and a continuous background prefetch to maintain K-V hitrate. The key metric is K-V hit ratio per session and effective bytes served from cache. If hitrate < ~70% you don't get batching benefits because you keep reloading large KV segments.
[03:18] Alex Mercer: Note that K-V prefetch aggressiveness trades memory and PCIe/NVLink traffic — on VPC/on-prem setups with limited NVLink you may see PCIe stalls. We provided a K-V warmup tool in the playbook we'll share.
[03:30] Liam O'Neal: Does quantization change K-V behavior? We considered int8 quant for long models.
[03:34] Priya Rao: Quant affects kernel selection and memory footprint. int8/int4 reduce KV size which helps hitrate and prefetch. But watch the kernel path: some int4 kernels are less optimized for large batch packing and could increase per-token latency for certain seq lengths — it's kernel-specific. Also sometimes the int4 runtime uses a different attention implementation that has different perf characteristics.
[03:54] Maya Chen: Ok, what are practical starting defaults for our profile? We need explicit numbers to test.
[03:58] Priya Rao: A prescriptive starting point: continuous_batching_window = 25ms, max_num_seqs = 48 per slot for 80GB A100-class; token_ceil_per_request = 1024 for short-priority pool, token_floor = 8, tenant_priority_window = 100ms. For longer generations, use a separate pool with max_num_seqs = 8 and batching_window = 40ms so long sequences get better memory contiguity.
[04:22] Sofia Petrov: Those numbers feel high on max_num_seqs; will that blow up memory for us?
[04:26] Diego Alvarez: Memory depends on per-seq KV footprint. For larger context 2k token sequences with 1.5MB per-seq KV, 48 seqs is huge. So we size it: if average KV per sequence is >200MB aggregate then reduce max_num_seqs accordingly. A quick rule: target aggregate KV memory usage < 60-70% of GPU memory.
[04:48] Liam O'Neal: How do you debug when throughput collapses? Our last incident had throughput drop and tail latencies spike for 20 minutes.
[04:56] Alex Mercer: First check KV hitrate metrics and batch assembly histograms. If you see high cold-miss rates you'll get lots of PCIe traffic and serialization. Also look at scheduler admission logs — sometimes a tenant consumes most sequences due to priority misconfig. We recommend enabling per-route tracing; we'll send a tracing snippet.
[05:15] Maya Chen: About VPC constraints — we have NVMe-backed nodes with 100Gb NICs. Would on-prem be fine or should we stay hosted?
[05:23] Priya Rao: On-prem can be fine but watch network topology: NVLink and intra-node bandwidth are most important. If your nodes have limited NVLink and must cross PCIe for KV transfers, that will add latency. Hosted Redwood Dedicated nodes are pre-tuned with local NVLink and kernel selection; on-prem customers often need an initial sizing & network audit.
[05:42] Liam O'Neal: Is there a test we can run to simulate token floods and long seq mixes?
[05:47] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we have a replay harness that can replay your traffic and synthetic burst overlays. It collects per-batch histograms, KV hitrates, and kernel-level occupancies. Priya will run the harness against your staging VPC to validate the recommended knobs.
[06:01] Maya Chen: Great. One more — what's the impact of enabling caching at the prefix level vs full KV cache? We sometimes have many repeated prompts with small prefixes.
[06:10] Priya Rao: Prefix caching is cheaper: you cache smaller prefix KV and you get quick wins for repeated short prompts. Full KV helps for long completions. Our platform supports hybrid: prefix-local cache for hot prefixes and a shared KV for longer contexts.
[06:22] Liam O'Neal: Perf regression safety — if we change quantization, how do we ensure LM quality is not worse?
[06:28] Alex Mercer: Redwood Optimize integrates small eval sets that can run A/B on model variants. We'll recommend a 2-step rollout: Perf-only bench in staging then gated quality evals on your holdout prompt set with statistical thresholds. If quality drops beyond tolerance we abort.
[06:42] Sofia Petrov: Any gotchas on autoscaling with these knobs? Autoscaler might spin up nodes that change scheduling behavior.
[06:48] Priya Rao: Autoscaling affects slot counts and therefore batch composition. When a new slot joins, batch sizes might shrink until it warms up. We recommend a slow ramp policy and slot warmup grace period where new slots are seeded with prewarm KV and don't immediately take high priority traffic.
[07:02] Maya Chen: Let's talk through a concrete failure mode: 2000 short requests arrive, plus 30 long ones. What do we see?
[07:09] Diego Alvarez: Short requests will be gathered into micro-batches; if continuous_batching_window is small they'll be issued fast with small batch sizes. Long ones will be appended but may wait if max_num_seqs is saturated. If token ceilings are enforced, long ones may be split across batches or moved to long-pool with lower priority.
[07:26] Liam O'Neal: How do we split long requests? Do you chunk on sequence level and keep KV continuity?
[07:31] Priya Rao: We can stream long completions by slicing output tokens and keeping KV cache between slices; the runtime maintains KV continuity. But slicing increases scheduling churn so balance carefully.
[07:45] Maya Chen: Is there a recommended prewarm routine after deploys to avoid cold misses at traffic surge?
[07:50] Alex Mercer: Yes: run a staged prewarm where you seed KV for the top 200 prefixes and replay 10-20% of expected peak QPS for 10 minutes. Then ramp to full traffic. Our playbook has a script for that.
[08:02] Sofia Petrov: On the numeric side, what's a typical drop in p95 after KV hitrate crosses 80%?
[08:08] Priya Rao: Observationally we see p95 drop by 2-3x when KV hitrate goes from ~50% to >80% for long workloads. For short workloads, benefits are less dramatic but p50 improves significantly.
[08:20] Liam O'Neal: How about token accounting for few-shot — if prompt includes many examples, will token_ceil force trimming or reject?
[08:27] Alex Mercer: Token_ceil applies to request contribution to a batch; for few-shot prompts you can enable a per-route prevalidation that either truncates or routes to a long-pool. We don't recommend silent truncation without owner consent.
[08:40] Maya Chen: Let's annotate the exact tests we want you to run in staging.
[08:44] Diego Alvarez: We'll run three staged tests: 1) steady-state mixed load at 1.2k QPS for 1 hour, 2) synthetic token-flood bursts overlayed (3k QPS for 15 minutes), 3) long-seq-heavy run with few-shot patterns. Each will collect batch histograms, KV hitrate, per-slot memory, and tail latency.
[09:02] Priya Rao: On the knobs we'll iterate: continuous_batching_window at [10ms,25ms,50ms], max_num_seqs at [16,32,48], token_ceil at [512,1024,2048]. We'll produce a matrix of results.
[09:16] Liam O'Neal: How long until we get the initial results?
[09:19] Alex Mercer: Priya should have benchmarks by 2026-01-22 if CloudScale provides the traffic trace by 2026-01-18.

--- mid-call noise & imperfect transcriptions ---

[45:22] Maya Chen: sorry there was a plane noise — can you repeat the part about NVLink vs PCI-e?
[45:28] Priya Rao: yeah NVLink avoids host roundtrips; if your on-prem nodes lack NVLink you'll pay a penalty when moving large KV chunks — that's what causes the 100-300ms tail spikes we saw in one bench for on-prem with PCIe-only fabric.

[55:03] Alex Mercer: Quick recap: recommended staging knobs, test matrix, and prewarm script. We'll also include prescriptive per-model/instance numbers in the doc.
[55:15] Maya Chen: Recap sounds good. Couple of infra asks — can you include the exact metric names and dashboard links to watch?
[55:22] Alex Mercer: Yes, we'll share dashboard templates: batch_assembly_histogram, kv_hitrate_ratio, per_slot_mem_bytes, kernel_occupancy_pct, and admission_rejections_count.
